text: How was this train station built? Forty sixth Street, Bliss Street stands on a concrete bridge from nineteen seventeen.
It started with the Dual Contracts of nineteen thirteen: a plan to push the subway into Queens.
The city wanted Queens Boulevard beautiful. So instead of a steel el, engineers chose reinforced concrete arches.
Footings went in first. Then crews poured concrete piers into wooden forms, around the clock.
Arches tied the piers together. Steel girders carried a deck for three tracks, with an express in the middle.
Then the station: two side platforms, canopies, and station houses tucked inside the viaduct.
On April twenty first, nineteen seventeen, the seven train rolled in.
In the fifties, the platforms grew for longer trains. But water seeped through the track bed, and the concrete crumbled.
From nineteen ninety three to ninety seven, the viaduct was rebuilt: forty thousand tons of concrete, new canopies, and stained glass.
In twenty eighteen, computer signals took over. Now it's being rebuilt again, with temporary platforms and two new elevators.
So, no grave yet. Congrats! You've discovered how forty sixth Street, Bliss Street was built.
